title: Shifted truncation reconstruction from a complete differential generator module
statement: Let $k$ be a commutative ring, $R$ a commutative $k$-algebra, $\mathfrak m\subseteq R$ an ideal, and $N$ an $R$-module. Assume the canonical map $\iota:N\to\varprojlim_{r\geq1}N/\mathfrak m^rN$, $z\mapsto(z\bmod\mathfrak m^rN)_r$, is an isomorphism. Let $\delta:R\to N$ be a $k$-derivation [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials], and assume $N$ is generated over $R$ by $\delta(x_1),\ldots,\delta(x_d)$ for some $d\geq0$ and $x_i\in R$. For $r\geq1$ set $R_r=R/\mathfrak m^r$, $C_r=\Omega_{R_r/k}$, with quotient-induced transition $\tau_r:C_{r+1}\to C_r$, and $C=\varprojlim_{r\geq1}C_r=\widehat\Omega_{R/k,\mathfrak m}$ [def-trf-continuous-kahler-differentials]. Suppose given $R$-linear maps $\phi_r:N\to C_r$ with $\tau_r\phi_{r+1}=\phi_r$ and $\phi_r\delta(x)=\mathrm d(x\bmod\mathfrak m^r)$ for every $x\in R$. Then $\delta(\mathfrak m^{r+1})\subseteq\mathfrak m^rN$ for every $r\geq1$, and there is a unique $R$-linear map $\eta_r:C_{r+1}\to N/\mathfrak m^rN$ with $\eta_r(\mathrm d(x\bmod\mathfrak m^{r+1}))=\delta(x)\bmod\mathfrak m^rN$ for all $x\in R$. Writing $\rho_r:N/\mathfrak m^{r+1}N\to N/\mathfrak m^rN$ and $\pi_r:N\to N/\mathfrak m^rN$ for quotient maps, one has $\rho_r\eta_{r+1}=\eta_r\tau_{r+1}$ and $\eta_r\phi_{r+1}=\pi_r$. Each $\phi_r$ induces $\bar\phi_r:N/\mathfrak m^rN\to C_r$, and $\bar\phi_r\eta_r=\tau_r$. The map $\Phi:N\to C$, $z\mapsto(\phi_r(z))_r$, is an isomorphism with inverse $\Psi((c_r)_r)=\iota^{-1}((\eta_r(c_{r+1}))_r)$; in particular $\Psi\Phi=\mathrm{id}_N$ and $\Phi\Psi=\mathrm{id}_C$.

source.place: Agent auxiliary reconstruction lemma based on Tag 02HQ (lemma-differential-mod-power-ideal), the Leibniz estimate for ideal powers, and Tag 00RO (lemma-universal-omega), the universal property. Extracts returned conormal proof Steps 5-8, including transition compatibility and both inverse identities; the original full argument is retained in report.md.

proof.text: Fix $r\geq1$. An element of $\mathfrak m^{r+1}$ is a finite sum of terms $a_0a_1\cdots a_{r+1}$ with $a_0\in R$ and $a_i\in\mathfrak m$ for $i>0$. Additivity and repeated Leibniz expansion give $\delta(a_0a_1\cdots a_{r+1})=(a_1\cdots a_{r+1})\delta(a_0)+\sum_{i=1}^{r+1}a_0\prod_{1\leq j\leq r+1,\,j\ne i}a_j\,\delta(a_i)$. Each coefficient lies in $\mathfrak m^r$, so each summand lies in $\mathfrak m^rN$. Summing proves $\delta(\mathfrak m^{r+1})\subseteq\mathfrak m^rN$.

source.place: Tag 02HQ (lemma-differential-mod-power-ideal), Leibniz estimate expanded for a module-valued derivation

proof.text: Put $Q_r=N/\mathfrak m^rN$. The rule $D_r(\bar x)=\delta(x)\bmod\mathfrak m^rN$ on $R_{r+1}$ is well defined by Step 1: two representatives differ by an element killed by the reduced derivation. It is additive, vanishes on $k$, and satisfies $D_r(\bar x\bar y)=\bar xD_r(\bar y)+\bar yD_r(\bar x)$ by reducing the corresponding equations for $\delta$. The scalar action on $Q_r$ factors through $R_{r+1}$ because $\mathfrak m^{r+1}N\subseteq\mathfrak m^rN$. Apply the universal bijection of [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] to this $k$-derivation: it gives a unique $R_{r+1}$-linear $\eta_r:C_{r+1}\to Q_r$ with the required values on $\mathrm d\bar x$. This is also uniqueness among $R$-linear maps, since both module actions factor through the surjection $R\to R_{r+1}$.

source.place: Tag 00RO (lemma-universal-omega), applied to the explicitly descended derivation

proof.text: For each of the given generators $\delta(x_i)$ of $N$, the assumed formula for $\phi_{r+1}$ and the defining formula for $\eta_r$ give $\eta_r\phi_{r+1}(\delta(x_i))=\delta(x_i)\bmod\mathfrak m^rN=\pi_r(\delta(x_i))$. Every $z\in N$ is a finite sum $\sum_{i=1}^d a_i\delta(x_i)$, so linearity gives $\eta_r\phi_{r+1}(z)=\pi_r(z)$. This also applies when $d=0$, since then $N=0$.

source.place: Agent calculation from the generation hypothesis and the defining formulas

proof.text: The $R$-action on $C_r$ factors through $R_r$, so $\mathfrak m^rC_r=0$. If $z\in\mathfrak m^rN$, write it as a finite sum of $az'$ with $a\in\mathfrak m^r$; $R$-linearity gives $\phi_r(z)=\sum a\phi_r(z')=0$. Thus $\bar\phi_r([z])=\phi_r(z)$ is well defined and linear on $Q_r$. For $x\in R$ the composite $\bar\phi_r\eta_r$ sends $\mathrm d(x\bmod\mathfrak m^{r+1})$ to $\phi_r\delta(x)=\mathrm d(x\bmod\mathfrak m^r)$, just as $\tau_r$ does. The explicit free-symbol quotient in [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] shows that these differentials generate $C_{r+1}$ over $R_{r+1}$ and hence over $R$ (all scalars lift to $R$). Consequently $\bar\phi_r\eta_r=\tau_r$.

source.place: Tag 00RO (lemma-universal-omega) and the preceding free-symbol construction; agent quotient calculation

proof.text: Both $\rho_r\eta_{r+1}$ and $\eta_r\tau_{r+1}$ have domain $C_{r+2}$ and codomain $Q_r$. On $\mathrm d(x\bmod\mathfrak m^{r+2})$ they both take the value $\delta(x)\bmod\mathfrak m^rN$, by the definitions of the quotient and differential transition maps. The differential-symbol generation in [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] therefore gives $\rho_r\eta_{r+1}=\eta_r\tau_{r+1}$. In particular for $c=(c_r)_r\in C$, $\rho_r\eta_{r+1}(c_{r+2})=\eta_r\tau_{r+1}(c_{r+2})=\eta_r(c_{r+1})$, so $(\eta_r(c_{r+1}))_r$ is a compatible element of $\varprojlim_r Q_r$.

source.place: Tag 00RO (lemma-universal-omega), generator test for the two displayed transition composites

proof.text: By [def-trf-continuous-kahler-differentials] the limit $C$ consists of compatible tuples with componentwise module operations. The assumed compatibility of $\phi_r$ therefore makes $\Phi(z)=(\phi_r(z))_r$ an $R$-linear map to $C$. Step 5 and the assumed isomorphism $\iota$ define the $R$-linear map $\Psi(c)=\iota^{-1}((\eta_r(c_{r+1}))_r)$. For $z\in N$, the $r$th coordinate of $\iota\Psi\Phi(z)$ equals $\eta_r\phi_{r+1}(z)=\pi_r(z)$ by Step 3; injectivity of $\iota$ gives $\Psi\Phi(z)=z$. Conversely the definition of $\Psi$ gives $\pi_r\Psi(c)=\eta_r(c_{r+1})$. Thus $\phi_r\Psi(c)=\bar\phi_r\pi_r\Psi(c)=\bar\phi_r\eta_r(c_{r+1})=\tau_r(c_{r+1})=c_r$ by Step 4 and compatibility of $c$. Equality of tuples gives $\Phi\Psi(c)=c$. These two identities prove that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism with exactly the stated inverse.
